summary: This work characterizes measurement-induced state transitions (MIST) in inductively-shunted transmon (IST) qubits, showing experimentally that the inductive shunt eliminates offset-charge dependence and stabilizes MIST compared to standard transmons. The results are explained using full quantum simulations and a modified semiclassical model that accounts for the IST's unbounded potential energy structure.
motivation: MIST becomes problematic during fast dispersive readout because it can leave qubits in high-energy states, and in transmons the MIST locations drift with offset charge, degrading quantum error correction performance. Adding an inductive shunt to the transmon offers an alternative solution by removing charge-offset dependence.
method: Two groups of inductively-shunted transmons (six qubits each, operating above and below the readout resonator) were fabricated with Josephson junction arrays providing the shunt inductance. MIST was measured by preparing qubits in $|0\rangle$ or $|1\rangle$, driving the readout resonator for $\sim 10/\kappa_r$, and measuring final qubit state as a function of resonator drive power and qubit frequency. Results were compared to full quantum (Lindblad) simulations and a renormalized semiclassical Floquet model.
result: Full quantum simulations with Hilbert space $\sim \bar{n} + 3\sqrt{\bar{n}}$ for the resonator and 18–24 IST levels showed good agreement with experimental MIST onsets and feature locations for both $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$ initial states; the modified semiclassical model (Eq. 6) reproduced essential features but underpredicted photon thresholds. Over 24 hours, MIST in IST qubits demonstrated qualitatively lower variability than Willow transmons at similar frequencies, confirming charge-noise immunity; $T_1$ values reached $\sim 100$ µs despite resonant defects.
